title: Answering an extract question
specPoints: Paper 1: the extract-based question on the play and on the novel; the method, practised on a Year 9 skills text

tips.title: Two bullets, two halves
tips.body: In this extract, and in the text as a whole. An answer that stays in the extract, however good, can be capped at the top of Level 2. Plan the move out before writing the move in.

tips.title: Idea first
tips.body: A sentence about the whole text that every paragraph serves: the light and what it costs. The Level 6 word is conceptualised, and it means the answer has an idea rather than a list.

tips.title: Methods on a stage
tips.body: Imagery, sentence forms, hyperbole, apostrophe, the soliloquy and its dramatic irony, the movement of scale within a speech, a stage direction. A play's methods include the ones only a stage has.

tips.title: Lines from memory, tied to a focus
tips.body: Closed book means the second bullet is carried in. For each set text keep a bank of exact lines, each tied to the moment and the idea it serves; two judicious ones beat six half-remembered.

tips.title: Context in a sentence, tied to a line
tips.body: Because the theatre played in daylight, the sun and stars are the lighting. A fact with a line attached explains a choice; a paragraph of history with no link shows only awareness of context, a lower-level descriptor.

tips.title: Fifty minutes, five to plan, five to check
tips.body: Half of Paper 1 for each question. On the Macbeth question four marks are for accuracy, so the last five minutes are for the full stops and the spellings.

why.matters: The extract question is the shape of half of the Literature exam, and it is the shape of reading a text closely while keeping the whole of it in mind: a passage in front of you, the rest carried in your head, and an idea that joins them. The method is learned once and applies to any play or novel, which is why the school teaches it in Year 9 on *Romeo and Juliet* before the set texts arrive. A reader who can start in a printed page and move out to the whole book, with exact lines and an idea of their own, has learned the thing that separates reading a text from remembering one.

examples.title: The scene everyone quotes
examples.body: Romeo under the window is the most quoted scene in English, and most people who quote it have never read what comes before or after. The extract question is the cure: start in the speech, then leave it for the Prologue that gives the ending and the choices that follow, and the scene reads differently. That habit of placing a famous passage in its whole is how a reader stops being carried by it.

examples.title: A passage in front of you, the whole in your head
examples.body: A lawyer with one clause and a whole contract, a doctor with one result and a whole history, a critic with one scene and a whole play: each is asked the extract question, what does this passage mean in the light of everything else. The method is the same, and the Year 9 version, practised on a balcony, is where it starts.

steps.title: The extract question: Paper 1's shape
steps.body:
Both halves of Literature Paper 1 ask the same kind of question. An extract from the set text is printed, a sentence says where in the text it comes from and what is happening, and the question begins *Starting with this extract*, or *this conversation*, or *this speech*: explore how the writer presents something. Two bullets follow: how the writer presents it in the extract, and how the writer presents it in the play, or the novel, as a whole.

**June 2024.** Macbeth: Act 1 Scene 7, the conversation in which Lady Macbeth persuades Macbeth to go on with the murder; starting with this conversation, explore how far Shakespeare presents Lady Macbeth as a strong female character. Jekyll and Hyde: an extract from Chapter 2, Utterson alone thinking about Hyde; starting with this extract, explore how Stevenson creates an atmosphere of fear and danger.

**The marks.** Thirty for each question: twelve for AO1, twelve for AO2, six for AO3, in six levels from 1 to 5 up to 26 to 30. The Shakespeare question adds four marks for AO4, spelling, punctuation and sentence structure. The paper is closed book: the extract is the only text in the room.

**The rule that caps.** The mark scheme names a response that does not address both the extract and the whole text as a rubric infringement, which can be capped at the top of Level 2. An answer that stays in the extract, however good, can be held to ten marks out of thirty.

steps.title: Start in the extract, and leave it
steps.body:
The method has three moves, and the question's wording gives all three.

**Read the extract with the question in hand.** The question names a focus: a character's strength, an atmosphere, a feeling. Mark the three or four moments in the extract that bear on it, and the method at each: an image, a sentence form, a stage direction, a shift.

**Plan the move out.** Two or three moments elsewhere in the text that bear on the same focus, with a line from memory for each, and the place they come from. This is what closed book means: the lines for the second bullet are carried in.

**Have an idea about the whole.** The top level calls it conceptualised: a sentence that says what the writer is doing with the focus across the text, which the extract paragraphs and the elsewhere paragraphs both serve.

**The shape on the page.** The idea; two or three paragraphs in the extract; two or three elsewhere; context where it explains a choice; the idea returned to. About fifty minutes, and five of them for the plan.

steps.title: The practice extract: Romeo under the window
steps.body:
The school teaches the extract question in Year 9 through *Romeo and Juliet*. AQA sets it as one of the Shakespeare options on Paper 1, but this school's students answer on *Macbeth*, so here the method is the point. This is the opening of Act 2 Scene 2, as the edition prints it. Romeo has climbed into the Capulets' garden after the feast; Juliet appears at a window above, not knowing he is there.

> **ROMEO.**\
> He jests at scars that never felt a wound.
>
> But soft, what light through yonder window breaks?\
> It is the east, and Juliet is the sun!\
> Arise fair sun and kill the envious moon,\
> Who is already sick and pale with grief,\
> That thou her maid art far more fair than she.\
> Be not her maid since she is envious;\
> Her vestal livery is but sick and green,\
> And none but fools do wear it; cast it off.\
> It is my lady, O it is my love!\
> O, that she knew she were!\
> She speaks, yet she says nothing. What of that?\
> Her eye discourses, I will answer it.\
> I am too bold, ’tis not to me she speaks.\
> Two of the fairest stars in all the heaven,\
> Having some business, do entreat her eyes\
> To twinkle in their spheres till they return.\
> What if her eyes were there, they in her head?\
> The brightness of her cheek would shame those stars,\
> As daylight doth a lamp; her eyes in heaven\
> Would through the airy region stream so bright\
> That birds would sing and think it were not night.\
> See how she leans her cheek upon her hand.\
> O that I were a glove upon that hand,\
> That I might touch that cheek.

**The question.** Starting with this speech, explore how Shakespeare presents Romeo's feelings for Juliet. Write about how Shakespeare presents his feelings in this speech, and in the play as a whole.

It rises from small things to large ones and ends with the heavens

steps.title: Methods in a speech, each with an effect
steps.body:
A speech gives the examiner a character alone with their feelings, and the methods are the ones that make feeling audible.

**Imagery.** “It is the east, and Juliet is the sun!” makes Juliet the source of light and warmth; “Arise fair sun and kill the envious moon” turns the metaphor into a command, and the moon, “sick and pale with grief”, is everything that is not her. The images do not decorate the feeling; they are how the feeling thinks.

**The question and the exclamation.** “But soft, what light through yonder window breaks?” is a question Romeo answers himself, and the exclamation on *sun* is the answer arriving. Sentence forms are methods on a stage too.

**Hyperbole.** “Two of the fairest stars in all the heaven”, and her eyes would outshine them. Exaggeration is how the speech measures the size of the feeling, and an audience is meant to smile at it and believe it at once.

**Apostrophe and the wish.** Romeo addresses the sun, the angel, the hand: “O that I were a glove upon that hand”. Speaking to what cannot answer is a method that shows a feeling with nowhere to go.

**The soliloquy itself.** He does not know she can hear; the audience does. The form gives the speech its honesty, and the dramatic irony gives it its charge.

steps.title: A top-level paragraph, and the move out
steps.body: One paragraph in the extract, then the sentence that leaves it. This is the shape of every paragraph pair in an extract answer.

visuals.problem: Write a paragraph on how Shakespeare presents Romeo's feelings in the speech, and then move to the play as a whole.

steps.text: The idea first: Shakespeare presents Romeo's feeling as a light that puts everything else in shadow, and the play will show what that costs.
steps.note: A conceptualised sentence: an idea about the whole, which the paragraph serves.

steps.text: In the extract: “It is the east, and Juliet is the sun!” makes Juliet the source of light, and “Arise fair sun and kill the envious moon” turns the metaphor into a command, so that the feeling gives orders to the sky; the moon, “sick and pale with grief”, is everything that is not her.
steps.note: Two references, the method named, the effect drawn: metaphor, command, contrast.

steps.text: Then the scale collapses: from the stars to “O that I were a glove upon that hand”. The feeling that began in the heavens ends as a wish to touch a cheek, and the movement is Shakespeare's way of making a feeling both cosmic and ordinary.
steps.note: A structural point within the speech: the movement of scale is a method.

steps.text: The move out: the audience already knows the cost, because the Prologue has told it that “A pair of star-cross'd lovers take their life”. Every image of light in this speech is heard against that, and the sun that kills the moon is a lover who will die.
steps.note: A line from elsewhere, from memory, tied to the same focus; the idea returned to.

steps.text: Context in a sentence: an Elizabethan audience, watching in daylight on an open stage, saw Juliet appear above on the gallery; the sun and the stars were the words that lit the scene, not the lamps.
steps.note: AO3 that explains a method: why the images have to do the lighting.

steps.title: Context that explains a choice
steps.body:
Six of the thirty marks are AO3: the relationship between the text and the contexts in which it was written. The mark scheme's top level asks for exploration of contextual factors shown by specific, detailed links between context, text and task; its lower levels describe awareness of contextual factors. The difference is whether the sentence links the context to something on the page.

**The stage.** Shakespeare's theatre played in daylight on a bare stage, and *Juliet appears above at a window* is a direction for the gallery at the back of it. The sun, the moon and the stars in Romeo's speech are the scene's lighting: the words do what the theatre could not.

**The poetry.** Lovers in the poems of Shakespeare's day praised a lady as a sun and her eyes as stars, and Romeo speaks that language fluently; whether he is feeling or performing is a question the play keeps open, and an answer can say so.

**The audience.** The Prologue tells them the ending before the play begins, so every image of light is heard by people who know the dark is coming.

**How to write it.** One sentence, tied to a line: *Because the theatre played in daylight, the sun and stars of the speech are its lighting.* Never a paragraph on Elizabethan England.

steps.title: Plan the other question
steps.body:
Later in the same scene Juliet, still not knowing Romeo is below, asks “O Romeo, Romeo, wherefore art thou Romeo?” and argues that “What's in a name? That which we call a rose” would smell as sweet by any other name.

Plan an answer to: *Starting with this speech, explore how Shakespeare presents Juliet as bold.* Five lines: the idea about the whole text; three moments in the speech with a method each; two moments elsewhere with a line each; one sentence of context tied to a line.

Then write the first paragraph pair: in the speech, and out of it.

steps.title: Conceptualised: an idea the whole answer serves
steps.body:
The Level 6 descriptor asks for a critical, exploratory, conceptualised response to the task and the whole text, with judicious references, fine-grained analysis of methods, and convincing exploration of contexts or interpretations.

**An idea first.** Not *Romeo has strong feelings for Juliet* but *Shakespeare presents Romeo's feeling as a light that puts everything else in shadow, and the play shows what that costs*. The extract paragraphs show the light; the elsewhere paragraphs show the cost.

**Judicious, from memory.** Two or three exact lines from elsewhere, chosen for the focus, beat six half-remembered ones.

**Fine-grained.** A method read for what it does at that moment: the command to the sun, the collapse of scale to a glove, the soliloquy's dramatic irony.

**An interpretation offered.** Is Romeo feeling or performing the language of love poetry? A sentence that holds the question open is the exploration of interpretations the descriptor names.

**On Macbeth, AO4 too.** Four marks for accuracy on the Shakespeare question: five minutes to check.

steps.title: The extract question in one page
steps.body:
One shape for both halves of Paper 1, practised here on the Year 9 play before it is used on *Macbeth* and *Jekyll and Hyde*.

- **The question:** starting with this extract, explore how the writer presents the focus; two bullets, the extract and the whole text; 30 marks, AO1 12, AO2 12, AO3 6, plus 4 for AO4 on Shakespeare.
- **The cap:** an answer that ignores the extract or the whole text can be capped at the top of Level 2.
- **Three moves:** in the extract, three or four moments with a method each; out of it, two or three lines from memory on the same focus; an idea about the whole that every paragraph serves.
- **Methods on a stage:** imagery, sentence forms, hyperbole, apostrophe, the soliloquy and its dramatic irony, the movement of scale within a speech.
- **Context in a sentence,** tied to a line: the daylight stage, the poetry of the day, a Prologue that gives the ending.
- **About fifty minutes,** five to plan, and five to check on the Shakespeare question.

Macbeth and Jekyll and Hyde each have their own topics; this is the method they share.

questions.solution: In this extract, and in the text as a whole: the two bullets are the two halves of the answer, and the mark scheme can cap a response that addresses only one at the top of Level 2.

questions.prompt: What is the term for a speech in which a character alone on stage speaks their thoughts aloud?
questions.solution: A soliloquy: thought spoken aloud to nobody, which makes it honest, and, when another character overhears, charged with dramatic irony. Romeo's speech under the window is one until Juliet speaks.

markScheme.description: soliloquy

questions.prompt: What does Romeo's command Arise fair sun and kill the envious moon do that the plain metaphor Juliet is the sun does not?
questions.solution: The metaphor names; the command acts. A feeling that gives orders to the sun and dismisses the moon as sick is a feeling that has taken over the speaker's world, and reading the second line for what it adds to the first is fine-grained analysis.

questions.prompt: Why is the movement from the stars to a glove upon that hand worth a paragraph?
questions.solution: Structure is a method in a speech as in a text: what comes first, where it moves, where it ends. The fall from the heavens to a glove is the speech's shape, and the shape is the feeling.

Because it is the last line of the extract, and the last line of any extract is always the most important one to analyse
The fall in scale is a structural method: a feeling in the language of the sky ends as a wish to touch a cheek

questions.solution: Judicious means chosen for the focus: a line elsewhere that bears on Romeo's feeling and reads the extract differently once it is in play. The Prologue does that; a line chosen for its act, its length or a different theme does not.

questions.solution: Apostrophe: speaking to what cannot reply, the sun, the angel, the hand. It is a method that shows a feeling with nowhere to go, and it is not the punctuation mark of the same name.

questions.prompt: A student writes: Shakespeare wrote in the 1590s under Elizabeth I, when the theatre was very popular and plays were performed in daylight. Where does the mark scheme place that sentence?
questions.solution: The top level asks for exploration of contextual factors shown by links between context, text and task. A fact with no line attached shows awareness and nothing more. The same fact, tied to the sun and stars as the scene's lighting, is context that explains.

Nowhere, because context is not assessed on Paper 1

questions.prompt: Why does the play keep open whether Romeo is feeling or performing the language of love poetry, and how does an answer use that?
questions.solution: Sun, stars, the lady as light: Romeo speaks the poetry of his day fluently, and the play will test whether the feeling outlasts the language. An answer that says so, without deciding, is exploring an interpretation, which Level 6 names.

markScheme.description: His images are the conventional ones of the love poetry of his day, so an answer can hold the question open as an interpretation

questions.prompt:
This is the opening of Act 2 Scene 2, as the edition prints it. Romeo has climbed into the Capulets' garden after the feast; Juliet appears at a window above, not knowing he is there.

> **ROMEO.**\
> He jests at scars that never felt a wound.
>
> But soft, what light through yonder window breaks?\
> It is the east, and Juliet is the sun!\
> Arise fair sun and kill the envious moon,\
> Who is already sick and pale with grief,\
> That thou her maid art far more fair than she.\
> Be not her maid since she is envious;\
> Her vestal livery is but sick and green,\
> And none but fools do wear it; cast it off.\
> It is my lady, O it is my love!\
> O, that she knew she were!\
> She speaks, yet she says nothing. What of that?\
> Her eye discourses, I will answer it.\
> I am too bold, ’tis not to me she speaks.\
> Two of the fairest stars in all the heaven,\
> Having some business, do entreat her eyes\
> To twinkle in their spheres till they return.\
> What if her eyes were there, they in her head?\
> The brightness of her cheek would shame those stars,\
> As daylight doth a lamp; her eyes in heaven\
> Would through the airy region stream so bright\
> That birds would sing and think it were not night.\
> See how she leans her cheek upon her hand.\
> O that I were a glove upon that hand,\
> That I might touch that cheek.

Starting with this speech, explore how Shakespeare presents Romeo's feelings for Juliet. Write the opening and the first paragraph pair of an answer: an idea about the whole text; a paragraph in the speech with two references, methods named and effects drawn; and the move out to one line from elsewhere in the play on the same focus, with a sentence of context tied to a line.
questions.solution: Shakespeare presents Romeo's feeling for Juliet as a light that puts everything else in shadow, and the play will show what that light costs. In the speech the feeling arrives as light before it arrives as a person: “But soft, what light through yonder window breaks?” is a question Romeo answers himself with an exclamation, “It is the east, and Juliet is the sun!”, and the metaphor is at once turned into a command, “Arise fair sun and kill the envious moon”, so that the feeling does not describe the sky but gives it orders; the moon, “sick and pale with grief”, becomes everything that is not Juliet. The images are how the feeling thinks, and they climb: her eyes would outshine “Two of the fairest stars in all the heaven”, and birds would sing at night. Then the scale collapses, from the heavens to “O that I were a glove upon that hand”, and a feeling stated in the language of the sky ends as a wish to touch a cheek; the movement is Shakespeare's method for making one feeling both cosmic and close. The audience hears all of it against a line it was given before the play began, “A pair of star-cross'd lovers take their life”: the sun that kills the moon is a lover who will die, and the light in this speech is already the light the ending will put out. Because Shakespeare's theatre played in daylight on a bare stage, with Juliet above on the gallery, the sun and the stars were the scene's lighting; the words did what the lamps could not, and the feeling that fills the sky here is the feeling the play will spend.

questions.prompt:
This is later in the same scene, after Romeo's speech under the window. Juliet, still not knowing Romeo can hear her, speaks from the window above.

> **JULIET.**\
> O Romeo, Romeo, wherefore art thou Romeo?\
> Deny thy father and refuse thy name.\
> Or if thou wilt not, be but sworn my love,\
> And I’ll no longer be a Capulet.
>
> **ROMEO.** *[Aside.]* Shall I hear more, or shall I speak at this?
>
> **JULIET.**\
> ’Tis but thy name that is my enemy;\
> Thou art thyself, though not a Montague.\
> What’s Montague? It is nor hand nor foot,\
> Nor arm, nor face, nor any other part\
> Belonging to a man. O be some other name.\
> What’s in a name? That which we call a rose\
> By any other name would smell as sweet;\
> So Romeo would, were he not Romeo call’d,\
> Retain that dear perfection which he owes\
> Without that title. Romeo, doff thy name,\
> And for thy name, which is no part of thee,\
> Take all myself.

Plan a full answer to: Starting with this speech, explore how Shakespeare presents Juliet as bold, using Juliet's speech in the same scene, from wherefore art thou Romeo to Take all myself. Give the idea about the whole text, three moments in the speech with a method and effect each, two moments elsewhere in the play with a line each, and one sentence of context tied to a line. Then write the paragraph on the speech in full.
questions.solution:
Idea: Shakespeare presents Juliet's boldness as reasoning, a girl who thinks her way to a decision out loud, and the play shows the decision costing her everything. In the speech: the repeated question, “O Romeo, Romeo, wherefore art thou Romeo?”, which is not a where but a why, so the audience hears her interrogating the world that separates them; the argument about the name, “What's in a name? That which we call a rose”, a piece of logic worked through in public, so her boldness is a mind and not a mood; the offer that ends it, take all myself, a decision made before Romeo has spoken a word to her. Elsewhere: the Prologue's star-cross'd lovers, which the audience holds against every bold decision she makes; and her later resolve in the play to act alone rather than be married against her will, the line the student carries in from memory. Context: a daughter in Shakespeare's Verona was expected to be given in marriage by her father, so a girl reasoning herself into a choice of husband on a balcony is bold by the standards of her stage as well as ours.

Paragraph. Juliet's boldness in the speech is the boldness of a mind at work. She does not know Romeo is below, so the repeated question “O Romeo, Romeo, wherefore art thou Romeo?” is asked of the night and not of him, and its word is why rather than where: she is interrogating the fact of his name, which is the fact of the feud. The speech then does something rarer on a stage than a declaration; it reasons. “What's in a name? That which we call a rose” would smell as sweet by any other name is an argument, worked step by step, that the name is no part of the man, and the audience hears a girl think her way past the thing that stands between them. The decision that closes the argument, to take all of him for her name, is made before Romeo has spoken, so that when he answers her the boldness has already happened. Shakespeare presents Juliet's boldness as intelligence spoken aloud, and the soliloquy form, with a listener she does not know about, lets the audience witness it before Romeo does.

examTechnique.body:
**Two bullets, both required.** In the extract and in the whole text; the mark scheme can cap an answer that addresses only one at the top of Level 2.

**Read the extract with the focus in hand;** mark three or four moments with a method each. Plan two or three lines from elsewhere on the same focus, from memory, before writing.

**Idea first.** One sentence about the whole text, served by every paragraph; the Level 6 word is conceptualised.

**Methods with effects,** including the ones only a stage has: the soliloquy, the direction, the movement of a speech.

**Context in a sentence tied to a line,** never a paragraph of history. About fifty minutes; five to plan; on the Macbeth question, five to check for AO4.
examinerErrors: Staying in the extract and never moving to the whole text, which the mark scheme can cap at the top of Level 2.
Retelling the extract rather than analysing methods and effects.
Opening with a summary of the play or an announcement of intent instead of an idea.
Half-remembered quotations from elsewhere that are not the text's words.
A paragraph of history or biography with no line attached, which is awareness of context rather than exploration.
Leaving the Macbeth question unchecked and losing the four AO4 marks to slips.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer opens with an idea about the whole text and lets the extract and the rest of the play serve it in turn. In the extract it reads three or four moments for their methods and effects, including the movement of a speech and the form of the scene; out of it, it brings two or three exact lines from memory on the same focus and reads the extract differently in their light. Context appears in sentences tied to lines, and an interpretation is held open where the text keeps it open. On the Macbeth question the last five minutes are given to accuracy, and the four marks for it are taken.
